readerTitle: A 2% defect rate: $800 a month, or $13,000?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (금속 브래킷 공장, 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 개념은 Juran·Feigenbaum의 품질 비용 이론에 근거
insight: 불량의 비용은 개수가 아니라 어디서 발견되느냐로 정해진다. 고객에게 닿은 소수의 불량이 비용 대부분을 만든다.
misconception: 불량 비용은 폐기한 부품 값(스크랩 보고서의 숫자)이다. 예방과 검사 비용은 아낄수록 이익이다.

sources.text: Juran, J. M. (1951). Quality Control Handbook. McGraw-Hill.
Feigenbaum, A. V. (1956). Total Quality Control. Harvard Business Review.
ASQ, Cost of Quality (prevention, appraisal, internal and external failure)

factChecks.note: 예방 사례: 센서가 유출 30개 중 20개를 기계에서 잡음. 개당 $400 → $4, 절감 20 × $396 = $7,920, 센서 비용 $2,000/월. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
Juran이 1950년대에 품질 비용 개념을 널리 알렸다는 서술과, 예방·평가·내부 실패·외부 실패 4분류가 Feigenbaum(1956)에서 비롯되었다는 점을 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 '널리 쓰이는 분류'로만 적었습니다.
ASQ Cost of Quality 페이지 URL이 유효한지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: A 2% defect rate: $800 a month, or $13,000?
body: A metal parts plant makes 10,000 brackets a month. About 2% come out bad. Each bracket costs $4 to make.
On the scrap report, that's $800. The real bill depends on one thing the report doesn't show: *where* each bad part was caught.

image.label: A bin of scrapped brackets beside a small price tag
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 공장 바닥의 작은 폐기 상자에 금속 브래킷 몇 개와 "$800" 가격표. 상자 뒤로 훨씬 큰 그림자가 벽에 드리워져 있고 그림자에 "?" 표시. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: What do the bad brackets really cost?
body: Of the 200 bad brackets each month, 120 are caught at the machine and scrapped. 50 are found at final inspection, after painting and packing. 30 reach customers, who need a rushed replacement and must sort their stock to find the bad ones.
Roughly what do bad parts cost the plant each month?

options.text: About $800, the cost of the parts themselves
options.feedback: This treats every bad part as $4 of material, as if all were caught at the machine. Parts caught later carry far more cost.

options.text: About $2,000, allowing for repainting and repacking
options.feedback: Right that later costs more, but this stops at the factory door. The 30 parts that escaped cost far more than the rest.
Yes. Most of the cost sits in the few parts that reached customers. The next card shows the math.

cards.title: Follow the 200 bad brackets.
body: The 30 escaped parts are 15% of the defects but about **92% of the cost**. The total is over 16 times the scrap report.

breakdown.label: Reached customers
breakdown.detail: 30 parts × $400: rush freight, replacement, customer sorting, admin

breakdown.label: Total per month
breakdown.detail: Compared with $800 on the scrap report

cards.title: The cost of poor quality
body: **The cost of poor quality** is all the money a business spends because work wasn't done right the first time: scrap, rework, extra checks, returns, refunds and lost customers.
Quality pioneer Joseph Juran helped popularize the idea in the 1950s. A widely used way to sort these costs has four buckets:
list: **Internal failure:** scrap and rework before shipping
**External failure:** returns, refunds, complaints, lost reorders
cards.callout: The last bucket is often the biggest and the hardest to see.
cards.softwareNote: Prevention is code review and automated tests. Internal failure is a bug found before release. External failure is the bug users hit: support tickets, refunds, churn and engineers pulled off planned work.

cards.title: Why late defects cost so much.
body: Every step a bad part passes through adds work to something that will be scrapped or redone. Paint, packing and freight are all spent on a part nobody can use.

Once it leaves your building, the cost spills into other people's time: your customer's staff sorting stock, your team on the phone, a rush truck. Then come costs no report records, like the reorder that quietly goes to a competitor.

image.label: Iceberg: scrap above water, failure costs below
image.brief: 빙산 인포그래픽. 수면 위 작은 부분에 "Scrap". 수면 아래 큰 부분에 위에서부터 "Rework", "Rush freight", "Customer sorting", "Staff time", 맨 아래 가장 크게 "Lost reorders". 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Spend earlier, spend less.
body: Suppose a $2,000-a-month sensor at the machine catches 20 of the 30 parts that used to escape. Those 20 now cost $4 each instead of $400.
Savings: 20 × $396 = **$7,920** a month, against $2,000 spent. Prevention shows up as a new line on the budget. Often it is cheaper than the failure it replaces, which never had its own line.

cards.title: Not every flaw is worth preventing.
body: Prevention and checks cost money too. Past a point, each extra check catches fewer problems than it costs, and it slows the work.

Focus on defects customers notice or that are expensive to fix late. A scratch on a hidden surface may not deserve a $2,000 sensor. And treat your estimates as rough: the goal is to see where the money goes, not to get the number exact.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your team ships updates weekly. Last month, three bugs in the payment page reached users. Each meant refunds, a flood of support tickets and engineers dropping planned work to patch it.
Your lead wants to cut testing time to ship features faster. What do you do?

options.text: Ship faster and fix bugs as users report them
options.feedback: You gain speed on paper, but every bug becomes an external failure: refunds, tickets and lost trust. Patching later also eats the time you saved.

options.text: Add automated tests and a review step for the payment code
options.feedback: This puts money into prevention where failures cost the most. A few releases slow down slightly to avoid the most expensive kind of bug.

options.text: Hire more support staff to handle bug reports faster
options.feedback: This softens the damage for users, but it spends more on failure instead of reducing it. The bugs keep coming.

cards.title: A defect's cost depends on where it's caught.
body: The scrap report shows the cheapest defects. The expensive ones are those your customers find.
**Try it today:** pick one recent mistake that reached a customer. List every cost it caused, from refunds to staff hours. Then ask where it could have been caught earlier.
